writingLibrary.title: 坚持锻炼的重要性
writingLibrary.prompt: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write a short essay on the importance of regular exercise. You should write at least 120 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
Nowadays, many college students spend long hours sitting in classrooms or in front of screens, and regular exercise is often neglected. In my view, physical activity is essential for both body and mind.

First, exercise strengthens the immune system and helps students keep fit. A simple thirty-minute jog several times a week can reduce the risk of common illnesses. Second, sports are an effective way to relieve stress. After intense study, playing basketball or doing yoga can refresh the mind and improve concentration in the next class. Finally, team sports teach cooperation and communication, which are valuable beyond campus.

In conclusion, universities should encourage students to form the habit of exercising. Only with a healthy body can we pursue academic goals more efficiently.

writingLibrary.title: 网络课程的利与弊
writingLibrary.prompt: Write an essay on online courses. You should write at least 120 words and comment on both advantages and disadvantages.
writingLibrary.essay:
Online courses have become an important part of campus life. While they bring clear benefits, they also present challenges.

On the one hand, web-based learning offers great flexibility. Students can review recorded lectures at their own pace and access courses from famous universities far away. This is especially helpful for those who need to balance part-time jobs and study. On the other hand, online classes require strong self-discipline. Without a real classroom atmosphere, some students easily get distracted by social media and fall behind.

Therefore, a blended model may work best: online resources for knowledge input, and offline discussion for deep understanding. Universities can also set clearer deadlines and interactive tasks to keep learners engaged.

writingLibrary.title: 宿舍生活与人际关系
writingLibrary.prompt: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay on how to get along with roommates. You should write at least 120 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
Dormitory life is an unforgettable part of college years, yet sharing a small room can sometimes lead to conflicts. Learning to get along with roommates is therefore a valuable lesson.

To begin with, respect for personal space and habits is fundamental. One should keep noise down at night and keep shared areas clean. Secondly, open communication prevents small misunderstandings from growing. If a problem appears, it is better to discuss it calmly instead of complaining behind someone's back. In addition, showing kindness in daily life—offering help when a roommate is ill, for example—builds trust over time.

In short, harmony in the dorm depends on respect, communication and care. These skills will also benefit our future work and family life.

writingLibrary.title: 选择专业还是兴趣
writingLibrary.prompt: Some people think students should choose a major by interest, while others prefer job prospects. Write an essay of at least 120 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
When filling in college applications, students often face a hard choice: follow interest or chase job prospects. Both views have their reasons.

Those who favor interest argue that passion keeps one motivated through difficult courses. A student who loves literature is more likely to read widely and write well. However, supporters of career planning point out that tuition and living costs are real. Majors with strong market demand may offer more internships and a smoother path to employment.

As far as I am concerned, the best solution is a balance. Students can choose a generally practical field and develop a serious interest within it. Career centers should also provide more guidance so that choices are based on facts rather than anxiety.

writingLibrary.title: 手机依赖
writingLibrary.prompt: Write an essay on smartphone addiction among young people. You should write at least 120 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
Smartphones bring convenience, but they also make many young people overly dependent. This phenomenon deserves attention.

The most obvious harm is wasted time. Endless short videos and notifications fragment our attention, making it hard to finish a book or a long assignment. Moreover, looking at the screen late at night damages sleep quality, which in turn affects memory and mood. Some students even feel anxious when the phone is not at hand.

To deal with this problem, we can start with small rules: putting the phone away during study, turning off non-essential notifications, and replacing some screen time with face-to-face talks. Technology should serve us, not control us. With conscious effort, we can enjoy the benefits of smartphones without becoming their slaves.

writingLibrary.title: 志愿服务
writingLibrary.prompt: Write an essay on the benefits of volunteer work for college students. Write at least 120 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
More universities now encourage students to take part in volunteer work. From tutoring children to helping at community events, such activities offer benefits beyond a line on a resume.

First, volunteering develops responsibility. When others rely on you, you learn to keep promises and manage time carefully. Second, it widens horizons. Meeting people from different backgrounds helps students understand real social needs instead of only textbook theories. Third, teamwork and communication skills grow naturally when volunteers cooperate under pressure.

Of course, study should still come first. Students need to choose programs that fit their schedule and interests rather than chasing certificates. When done properly, volunteer work can become one of the most valuable teachers on campus.

writingLibrary.title: 低碳生活
writingLibrary.prompt: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay on low-carbon life. You should write at least 120 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
Climate change is no longer a distant topic. A low-carbon lifestyle, starting from daily choices, is something college students can practice now.

Small actions matter. Carrying a reusable bottle and shopping bag reduces plastic waste. Choosing buses, subways or bicycles instead of short taxi rides cuts emissions. Turning off lights and unplugging chargers when leaving the dorm saves energy. If many students follow these habits, the collective effect will be significant.

Meanwhile, campuses can support green living by installing more recycling bins and water refill stations. Courses and clubs may also raise awareness through practical projects.

In conclusion, a low-carbon life does not require dramatic sacrifice. It asks for consistent, sensible choices. Protecting the environment is protecting our own future.

writingLibrary.title: 考试作弊问题
writingLibrary.prompt: Write an essay on why students cheat in exams and how to stop it. At least 120 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
Academic dishonesty, especially cheating in exams, remains a problem on some campuses. Understanding its causes is the first step toward a solution.

Some students cheat because they leave revision until the last minute and fear failure. Others follow peers under wrong social pressure. Weak supervision and overly heavy course loads may also play a role.

To reduce cheating, punishment alone is not enough. Teachers should design assessments that test understanding rather than memorization, for example open-book questions or project-based work. Students, for their part, need to treat grades as feedback, not as the only measure of self-worth. A culture of integrity is built gradually—through clear rules, fair exams, and honest role models.

True confidence comes from real ability, not from a copied answer.

writingLibrary.title: 阅读习惯
writingLibrary.prompt: Some people say print books are dying. Write your opinion on reading habits in the digital age. At least 120 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
With e-books and audio programs everywhere, some claim that print books are dying. In my view, the form of reading may change, but the habit of deep reading is more important than ever.

Digital reading is convenient for search and portability. News, novels and textbooks can all fit into one device. However, screens also invite multitasking, and long serious works often suffer when attention jumps between apps. Paper books, by contrast, create a quiet physical space that many readers find helpful for concentration.

What really matters is choosing the right medium for the purpose. Skimming updates on a phone is fine; studying a classic may deserve a printed copy and a notebook. Schools should still teach slow, careful reading so that technology expands our minds instead of shortening them.

writingLibrary.title: 兼职的利弊
writingLibrary.prompt: Write an essay on college students taking part-time jobs. Give your opinion. At least 120 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
Taking a part-time job is common among college students. Whether it is wise depends on how the work is arranged.

A suitable job can teach time management and practical skills that classrooms rarely cover. Earning some money also eases family pressure and builds independence. Yet if work hours are too long, grades and health may decline. Some low-end jobs offer little learning and mainly consume energy.

Therefore, students should set clear priorities. Study remains the main task. A job close to one's major, or one that trains communication and responsibility, is preferable. Limiting weekly hours and choosing flexible shifts helps keep a balance.

Part-time work is a tool, not a goal. Used wisely, it enriches college life; used blindly, it becomes a burden.

writingLibrary.title: 人工智能与学习
writingLibrary.prompt: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay on how artificial intelligence should be used in university study. You should write at least 150 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping how university students learn. Used thoughtfully, AI tools can deepen understanding; used carelessly, they may weaken original thinking.

On the positive side, intelligent tutors can explain difficult concepts repeatedly and provide instant feedback on language practice. Data analysis tools help students process large information sets in research projects. These advantages free time for higher-level questions that machines cannot ask for us.

However, over-reliance is a real risk. If essays and problem sets are simply generated by AI, students may lose the ability to construct arguments and solve unfamiliar problems. Academic integrity also demands transparent use of such tools.

A sensible policy is to treat AI as a laboratory partner rather than a substitute brain. Universities should teach prompt design, fact-checking and ethical boundaries, while assessments focus on reasoning processes. In this way, technology multiplies human potential instead of replacing it.

writingLibrary.title: 城市绿色空间
writingLibrary.prompt: Write an essay on the role of urban green spaces in modern cities. At least 150 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
As cities densify, parks and tree-lined streets are not luxuries but necessities. Urban green spaces support public health, climate resilience and social life.

Research associates nearby parks with lower stress levels and more physical activity. For office workers and students, a short walk among trees can restore attention more effectively than another cup of coffee. Green cover also reduces the urban heat island effect and absorbs rainfall, easing pressure on drainage systems during storms.

Yet equity remains a challenge. Low-income neighborhoods often have fewer trees and smaller playgrounds. City planning should therefore prioritize planting and park investment where vulnerability and heat are highest, rather than only in wealthy districts.

Green space is infrastructure for well-being. When governments treat it as seriously as roads and wires, cities become healthier places to study, work and grow old.

writingLibrary.title: 远程办公的未来
writingLibrary.prompt: Some believe remote work will become the norm. Discuss its benefits and limits. At least 150 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
The pandemic accelerated remote work, and years later a hybrid pattern dominates many knowledge industries. Whether it becomes the full norm depends on the nature of work.

Remote arrangements cut long commutes and allow talent to live in lower-cost cities. Parents and people with disabilities often gain better access to stable employment. Documentation culture can also improve when teams must write things down.

Nevertheless, fully remote models struggle with spontaneous collaboration and onboarding of new hires. Careers may stall if visibility drops, and company culture is harder to transmit through screens alone. Some tasks—hardware labs, certain client meetings—still need shared physical space.

The most durable future is likely flexible: clear outcomes, protected deep-work time, and deliberate in-person moments for trust-building. Organizations that design remote work as a system, not as a temporary perk, will attract and keep skilled people.

writingLibrary.title: 消费主义与年轻人
writingLibrary.prompt: Write an essay on consumerism among young people and how to form rational consumption. At least 150 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
From limited sneakers to latest phones, young consumers face intense marketing. While spending can express identity, unchecked consumerism brings financial stress and environmental costs.

Social media amplifies comparison. When feeds are full of curated lifestyles, ordinary income may feel insufficient, pushing some toward installment loans or even illegal lending. The result is anxiety rather than lasting satisfaction. Fast fashion and disposable gadgets also pile up waste.

Rational consumption starts with values. Students can distinguish needs from wants, set a monthly budget, and prefer quality that lasts. Campuses may offer financial literacy courses and second-hand exchanges. Brands, for their part, should be regulated against misleading advertising targeting minors.

Enjoying material comfort is not shameful. The problem begins when purchases define self-worth. A mature consumer spends on life, not on images of life.

writingLibrary.title: 全球化与文化多样性
writingLibrary.prompt: Discuss how globalization affects cultural diversity. At least 150 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
Globalization connects markets and minds, but its effect on cultural diversity is double-edged.

On one hand, shared platforms let minority music, films and cuisines reach global audiences. Translation tools and travel make cross-cultural friendship easier. Young people can study abroad and return with hybrid identities that enrich local scenes.

On the other hand, dominant languages and entertainment industries may crowd out smaller traditions. Dialects fade when education and media reward only a standard tongue. Tourist packaging can turn living culture into a performance that loses meaning.

Protecting diversity does not mean isolating cultures. It means fair resources for local languages, support for creators outside megacities, and education that teaches both global competence and local heritage. A healthy world system resembles a forest: many species, not a single lawn.

writingLibrary.title: 终身学习
writingLibrary.prompt: Why is lifelong learning important in a rapidly changing economy? At least 150 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
Industries transform faster than degree programs can be rewritten. In such an economy, graduation is a starting line, not a finish line. Lifelong learning has become a professional survival skill.

New tools appear every few years. Professionals who update their methods regularly remain employable; those who rely only on knowledge from their twenties risk sudden obsolescence. Learning also supports career shifts—teachers become instructional designers, engineers move into product management.

Still, continuous study is not simply collecting certificates. Effective lifelong learners choose problems worth solving, practice deliberately, and share results with communities. Employers can help by funding training and recognizing internal mobility rather than punishing curiosity.

Governments should treat adult education as infrastructure: affordable courses, flexible schedules, and portable credentials. When societies make learning ordinary, individuals face change with confidence instead of fear.

writingLibrary.title: 社交媒体与公共讨论
writingLibrary.prompt: Write an essay on how social media influences public discussion. At least 150 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
Social media promised a global public square. What emerged is powerful for mobilization yet fragile for serious debate.

Speed and reach help citizens share eyewitness information and organize aid during crises. Marginalized voices can find audiences that traditional media ignored. These are real democratic gains.

Yet algorithmic feeds often reward outrage over nuance. Complex policy issues collapse into slogans, and misinformation spreads faster than corrections. Filter bubbles may harden identities until opponents are seen as enemies rather than fellow citizens.

Improving the square requires several layers: platforms should rank for reliability, not only engagement; schools must teach media literacy; users need habits of pausing before sharing. Offline forums—libraries, town halls—still matter for slower, embodied dialogue.

Technology alone cannot guarantee a healthy public sphere. Design, education and civic culture must work together.

writingLibrary.title: 延迟满足与成功
writingLibrary.prompt: Some argue that delayed gratification predicts success more than IQ. Comment on this view. At least 150 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
The famous marshmallow experiments suggested that children who wait for a larger reward often do better later. While the story is oversimplified, the core idea—self-regulation matters—remains useful.

Delayed gratification is not mere denial. It is the skill of aligning today's choices with tomorrow's goals: saving instead of impulse buying, practicing instead of endless gaming. In university, that skill shows up as steady revision rather than last-minute panic.

However, success is not only personal grit. Opportunity structures—family resources, school quality, health—shape what "waiting" can achieve. Blaming individuals for systemic barriers is unfair.

A balanced view treats self-control as trainable and environment as adjustable. Students can practice implementation intentions and environment design; institutions can reduce unnecessary stressors. Together, patience and fair conditions make long-term goals reachable.

writingLibrary.title: 文化遗产保护
writingLibrary.prompt: Write an essay on protecting cultural heritage in the face of urbanization. At least 150 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
Old streets and craft traditions often stand in the path of new roads and towers. Protecting heritage is not nostalgia alone; it is keeping a city's memory and identity alive.

Heritage sites attract thoughtful tourism and teach history more vividly than textbooks. Traditional techniques can also inspire contemporary design. When neighborhoods are demolished wholesale, social networks and intangible culture disappear with them.

Yet freezing a city in time is neither possible nor desirable. Adaptive reuse—turning warehouses into libraries, repairing temples for community use—can balance preservation and development. Clear laws, public consultation and funding for maintenance are essential.

Citizens play a role too: documenting oral history, supporting local crafts, and demanding transparency in planning. Cities that honor layers of time tend to be more livable than those that erase them for short-term gain.

writingLibrary.title: 睡眠与学习效率
writingLibrary.prompt: Many students sacrifice sleep for study. Discuss the consequences and solutions. At least 150 words.
writingLibrary.essay:
All-nighters before exams are common, yet sleep research suggests they often backfire. Memory consolidation depends on adequate rest, so cutting sleep can erase what was just crammed.

Short-term, tired students show weaker working memory, slower reaction times and poorer emotional regulation. Over months, irregular schedules disrupt circadian rhythms, raising risks of anxiety and metabolic problems. Coffee cannot fully compensate.

Solutions must be structural as well as personal. Campuses can avoid early high-stakes exams after late events and educate students about sleep as a study skill. Study groups should not pressure members into overnight marathons. Individually, a consistent bedtime, limited late caffeine and phone-free wind-down routines help.

High performance is not the opposite of rest; it depends on it. Treat sleep as part of the syllabus, and grades often improve without longer hours at the desk.

writingLibrary.title: 早起与作息
writingLibrary.prompt:
Some students prefer getting up early; others stay up late. Which is better for study?

(参考题型: Early Birds or Night Owls?)
writingLibrary.essay:
Whether one studies best at dawn or at midnight depends on the person, but irregular schedules usually hurt more than they help.

Early risers often report quieter mornings and fewer interruptions. A fixed early routine can free time for exercise and breakfast, both of which support concentration. Night owls, however, may find their minds sharper after dark when campuses grow quiet.

The real enemy is inconsistency. Sleeping at wildly different hours confuses the body clock and weakens memory. Students should discover their natural peak time, protect a stable sleep window, and avoid all-nighters before exams.

In short, choose the rhythm you can keep, not the one that looks impressive online. Steady habits beat heroic bursts.

writingLibrary.title: 课堂出勤
writingLibrary.prompt:
Should class attendance be mandatory? Give your views.

(参考题型: On Mandatory Attendance)
writingLibrary.essay:
Some universities require attendance; others leave it to students. Both sides have merit.

Supporters argue that showing up builds discipline and exposes learners to discussion they cannot get from slides. Teachers also receive feedback from faces in the room. Critics reply that mature students should manage their own time, and that forced attendance fills seats without filling minds.

A middle path works best: require presence for labs and presentations, allow flexibility for large lectures if assignments are submitted, and improve teaching quality so students want to come.

Attendance policy should serve learning, not bureaucracy. When classes are worth attending, numbers take care of themselves.

writingLibrary.title: 共享单车
writingLibrary.prompt:
Write a short essay on shared bicycles in cities.

(参考题型: Shared Bicycles on Campus and Beyond)
writingLibrary.essay:
Shared bicycles solved the "last mile" problem for many students. A short ride between the dorm and the library can save bus time and money.

Problems appear when bikes are dumped on sidewalks or locked privately. Management companies must rebalance fleets, while users need basic rules: park in marked areas, report broken locks, and ride safely in traffic.

Universities can help by marking parking zones near gates and teaching road safety during orientation. Responsible use keeps the system cheap and available.

Shared mobility is a public good only when the public treats it as one.

writingLibrary.title: 兴趣爱好
writingLibrary.prompt:
Why are hobbies important for college students?

(参考题型: Hobbies Beyond the Syllabus)
writingLibrary.essay:
A timetable full of courses is not a complete education. Hobbies restore energy and sometimes open careers.

Music, sports, cooking, or coding for fun train patience and creativity. They also create social circles beyond one's major, which is valuable in a world of cross-disciplinary work.

The risk is turning hobbies into yet another competition. A weekend hike does not need an audience. Students should keep at least one activity that exists for joy alone.

Balance is not a luxury; it is a study skill in disguise.

writingLibrary.title: 第一印象
writingLibrary.prompt:
Do first impressions matter in social life?

(参考题型: The Weight of First Impressions)
writingLibrary.essay:
First impressions form quickly through clothing, tone, and eye contact. They influence interviews and friendships more than we admit.

Yet snap judgments are often wrong. Quiet people may be deep thinkers; nervous speakers may know the material well. Relying only on first minutes creates unfair bias.

Wise social practice is two-sided: present yourself carefully when it matters, and give others time beyond the first meeting.

Impressions open doors; character keeps them open.

writingLibrary.title: 口头报告
writingLibrary.prompt:
How can students give better oral presentations?

(参考题型: Speaking to the Room)
writingLibrary.essay:
A good presentation starts weeks before the microphone. Structure first: one clear message, three supporting points, a short story or example.

Practice aloud until timing feels natural. Slides should support speech, not replace it. During delivery, slow down, look at people rather than the screen, and pause after key ideas.

Questions are gifts, not attacks. If you do not know an answer, say so and promise a follow-up.

Confidence is preparation made visible.

writingLibrary.title: 食堂浪费
writingLibrary.prompt:
What can be done to reduce food waste in canteens?

(参考题型: Finishing What We Take)
writingLibrary.essay:
Canteen waste is visible every evening: trays of rice and vegetables thrown away. Solutions are simple but need consistency.

Offer smaller portion prices, allow half-rice orders, and place reminders that taking less is smarter than dumping more. Student volunteers can weigh waste weekly and post results.

Culture shifts when finishing a reasonable plate becomes normal rather than heroic.

Food waste is an ethical issue long before it is an environmental report.

writingLibrary.title: 理想工作
writingLibrary.prompt:
What qualities matter most in an ideal job?

(参考题型: Beyond Salary)
writingLibrary.essay:
Young graduates often weigh salary first, then discover other factors dominate daily satisfaction.

Opportunity to learn, respectful teammates, and a manager who gives clear feedback predict happiness better than a small pay gap. Meaning matters too: work that aligns with values sustains energy during hard months.

No job is perfect. The practical approach is to rank what you will not compromise on for the next three years.

Choose a job that grows you, not only one that photographs well.

writingLibrary.title: 礼貌与尊重
writingLibrary.prompt:
Why do politeness and respect still matter?

(参考题型: Small Words, Large Effects)
writingLibrary.essay:
Please, thank you, and sorry are tiny words with large social effects. They signal that another person's time counts.

Politeness is not weakness. In conflict, calm language lowers temperature and makes solutions possible. Online, where tone disappears easily, careful wording matters even more.

Schools can model respect in how teachers speak to students; families model it at dinner tables.

Civil behavior is infrastructure for cooperation.

writingLibrary.title: 考试压力
writingLibrary.prompt:
How should students deal with exam pressure?

(参考题型: Pressure, Not Panic)
writingLibrary.essay:
Exam pressure is universal. The goal is not to eliminate nerves but to keep them useful.

Break revision into small targets, use past papers under timed conditions, and sleep before the test rather than memorizing until dawn. Breathing exercises reduce physical panic.

If anxiety becomes overwhelming, counseling centers exist for a reason—asking for help is strength.

Preparation plus self-care is the only reliable formula.

writingLibrary.title: 校园卡与消费
writingLibrary.prompt:
Comment on cashless payment on campus.

(参考题型: Wallet-Free Campus)
writingLibrary.essay:
Mobile pay now covers dining halls, laundries, and copy shops on many campuses. Benefits include speed and a clear digital record of spending.

Risks include overspending when money feels abstract and security problems if a phone is lost. Students should enable lock screens, check weekly bills, and keep a small cash backup.

Convenience is real; mindfulness is still required.

writingLibrary.title: 选修课
writingLibrary.prompt:
What is the value of elective courses?

(参考题型: Electives as Exploration)
writingLibrary.essay:
Major courses build depth; electives build width. A computer science student who takes design or psychology learns to see users, not only code.

Electives also allow low-risk testing of new interests before committing careers.

The strategy is simple: choose at least one elective far from your major each year, and treat it seriously rather than as an easy grade.

Breadth is not distraction; it is future adaptability.

writingLibrary.title: 宿舍网络
writingLibrary.prompt:
Should dorm internet be limited at night?

(参考题型: Night Internet, Day Grades)
writingLibrary.essay:
Some dorms cut internet after midnight; others keep it open. Both aim at student well-being.

Night cutoffs protect sleep but frustrate night owls and group projects across time zones. Full freedom assumes self-control that not everyone has yet.

A softer model—bandwidth throttling, quiet-hour reminders, and education on sleep—often works better than hard bans.

Rules should teach habits, not only enforce them.

writingLibrary.title: 第二外语
writingLibrary.prompt:
Is learning a second foreign language worthwhile?

(参考题型: One More Language, One More Window)
writingLibrary.essay:
English is necessary but no longer sufficient for many roles. A second language—Spanish, Japanese, Arabic—opens markets and research.

Even without fluency, beginner-level skills show employers that you can learn complex systems.

Language study also softens cultural arrogance: grammar forces you to see the world through another logic.

Start small, stay consistent, and use the language for real tasks.

writingLibrary.title: 假期规划
writingLibrary.prompt:
How should students plan winter or summer vacation?

(参考题型: Rest That Restores)
writingLibrary.essay:
Long breaks fail in two ways: total collapse into screens or overpacked resume-building.

A balanced plan includes real rest, one skill project, part-time work or volunteering, and unhurried family time.

Write a loose weekly plan before the break starts; leave free days empty on purpose.

Vacation is not wasted time. It is when the next semester's energy is banked.

writingLibrary.title: 名牌与身份
writingLibrary.prompt:
What do you think of brand-name obsession among young people?

(参考题型: Names on Clothes, Values on Us)
writingLibrary.essay:
Brand names can signal quality, but obsession confuses logos with worth.

Social comparison online makes ordinary incomes feel inadequate. The cure is not forced poverty but clarity: buy quality when it lasts, refuse debt for status, and invest in skills that cannot be worn out.

Identity is built through actions over years, not through seasonal collections.

writingLibrary.title: 电子词典与手机
writingLibrary.prompt:
Are paper dictionaries obsolete?

(参考题型: Dictionary Wars)
writingLibrary.essay:
Phones beat paper on speed. Students can look up words mid-reading without losing place.

Yet the friction of a paper dictionary sometimes deepens memory, and specialized dictionaries explain usage better than first-page search results.

Practical answer: use digital tools for daily study, keep one good learner's dictionary for serious writing, and review looked-up words rather than collecting screenshots.

Tools matter less than the habit of review.

writingLibrary.title: 宿舍卫生
writingLibrary.prompt:
How can roommates share cleaning fairly?

(参考题型: Fair Chores, Calm Rooms)
writingLibrary.essay:
Shared rooms fail when cleaning depends on mood. Solutions are almost boring: a visible rotation chart, clear standards for the bathroom and floor, and a ten-minute weekly reset together.

If someone repeatedly skips chores, address it calmly with facts rather than group chat gossip.

A clean room is not about perfection; it is about respect for shared air.

writingLibrary.title: 英语角
writingLibrary.prompt:
Are English corners useful?

(参考题型: Practice That Speaks Back)
writingLibrary.essay:
English corners help when they force real speaking, not only listening to advanced peers.

Smaller groups, themed topics, and patient facilitators lower anxiety. Beginners should prepare two sentences before arriving.

Usefulness rises when participants give gentle feedback instead of silent judgment.

Language grows through use, even imperfect use.

writingLibrary.title: 成绩与能力
writingLibrary.prompt:
Do grades always reflect ability?

(参考题型: Grades as Signals)
writingLibrary.essay:
Grades summarize performance in a course under given rules. They signal effort and some skills, but miss creativity, collaboration, and late-blooming talent.

Employers increasingly ask for projects and portfolios alongside transcripts.

Students should treat grades as feedback, not identity. Improve weak areas without believing a single number defines you.

Ability is a trajectory; grades are snapshots.

writingLibrary.title: 算法推荐与信息茧房
writingLibrary.prompt:
Discuss how recommendation algorithms shape what we read.

(参考题型: Feed the Mind, Not Only the Feed)
writingLibrary.essay:
Recommendation systems save time by surfacing content similar to what we already like. The cost is narrower exposure: complex viewpoints are filtered out as "uninteresting."

This is not merely individual weakness. Design choices optimize engagement, often amplifying outrage.

Countermeasures include following diverse sources, using chronological modes when available, and reading long-form analysis weekly. Schools should teach algorithmic literacy as part of media education.

A healthy mind diets on information the way a healthy body diets on food—variety included.

writingLibrary.title: 数据隐私
writingLibrary.prompt:
Why does personal data privacy matter for ordinary users?

(参考题型: The Value of Quiet Data)
writingLibrary.essay:
Apps request contacts, location, and photos for convenience. Users often consent without reading.

Personal data can reveal habits, finances, and social graphs. Once leaked, it cannot be "unleaked."

Practical hygiene: limit permissions, prefer services with clear privacy policies, and avoid reusing passwords. Regulators must punish deceptive design, not only breaches.

Privacy is not secrecy; it is control over context.

writingLibrary.title: 远程教育公平
writingLibrary.prompt:
Has remote education widened or narrowed inequality?

(参考题型: Remote Does Not Mean Equal)
writingLibrary.essay:
Remote classes reached students during lockdowns, but outcomes diverged. Learners with quiet rooms, fast internet, and supportive adults progressed; others struggled with shared devices and noisy homes.

Access to a login is not access to learning. Schools need loaner devices, offline materials, and flexible deadlines.

Technology is an equalizer only when institutions fund the conditions around it.

writingLibrary.title: 城市通勤与住房
writingLibrary.prompt:
How do long commutes affect quality of life?

(参考题型: The Hidden Cost of Distance)
writingLibrary.essay:
Long commutes steal hours from sleep, exercise, and family. Research links extreme commuting with stress and lower life satisfaction.

Housing prices push workers outward; employers cluster downtown. Solutions include remote-work days, transit investment, and mixed-use zoning so jobs exist near homes.

Urban planning is lifestyle policy in concrete form.

writingLibrary.title: 消费信贷与青年
writingLibrary.prompt:
What are the risks of easy consumer credit for young adults?

(参考题型: Borrowed Lifestyles)
writingLibrary.essay:
Installment apps make expensive phones feel affordable until interest stacks. Young earners with unstable income are especially vulnerable.

Prevention combines product regulation—clear APR labels, cooling-off periods—and financial literacy that teaches budgeting before slogans about "living fully."

Debt can finance growth (education, tools) or fantasy (status goods). Knowing the difference is adulthood.

writingLibrary.title: 文化遗产数字化
writingLibrary.prompt:
Does digitizing heritage save or dilute it?

(参考题型: Pixels and Memory)
writingLibrary.essay:
High-resolution scans let a student in another province study a fragile manuscript. Virtual museums expand access during disasters and pandemics.

Yet a flattened image is not a temple: smell, scale, and community ritual disappear. Digitization without context becomes tourism screenshots.

Best practice pairs digital archives with living communities and physical conservation budgets.

Code can carry memory; only people can keep it meaning.

writingLibrary.title: 职场终身雇佣的终结
writingLibrary.prompt:
Is the idea of a "job for life" still realistic?

(参考题型: Careers as Portfolios)
writingLibrary.essay:
Lifetime employment has shrunk in most private sectors. Projects reorganize, firms merge, and automation reshapes roles.

Workers now need portable skills, networks, and savings buffers. Employers who still promise loyalty must offer growth in return.

This is not pure instability; it can reward curiosity. But societies need safety nets for transitions—training accounts, portable benefits.

Plan for change even while performing well today.

writingLibrary.title: 睡眠不足的社会成本
writingLibrary.prompt:
Beyond personal health, what does sleep deprivation cost society?

(参考题型: When Cities Never Sleep)
writingLibrary.essay:
Sleep loss is not only private. Tired drivers crash; fatigued doctors err; exhausted students learn less and create long-term public costs.

Shift work, late-night culture, and always-on messaging normalize exhaustion.

Policy responses include limits on excessive overtime, later school start times, and public campaigns that treat sleep as safety infrastructure.

Rest is productivity's foundation, not its enemy.

writingLibrary.title: 语言濒危与方言保护
writingLibrary.prompt:
Why should societies protect minority languages?

(参考题型: Languages as Ecosystems)
writingLibrary.essay:
Each language encodes unique ways of classifying nature, kinship, and time. When a language dies, libraries die with it.

Globalization favors dominant tongues, but protection is possible: bilingual education, community media, and documentation projects led by native speakers.

Symbolic recognition without resources changes little. Living languages need daily use in schools and services.

Diversity of speech is diversity of mind.

writingLibrary.title: 科研评价与论文压力
writingLibrary.prompt:
How do publication metrics affect research quality?

(参考题型: Counting the Wrong Things)
writingLibrary.essay:
Universities often reward paper counts and journal brands. The pressure can encourage salami-slicing, rushed methods, and fashionable topics over necessary ones.

Alternative metrics—open data, replication, societal impact—are harder but more honest.

Individual researchers can still choose integrity; institutions must make that choice viable.

Science advances when curiosity leads and numbers follow.

writingLibrary.title: 老龄化与科技
writingLibrary.prompt:
How can technology support aging populations?

(参考题型: Designing for Longer Lives)
writingLibrary.essay:
Wearables can flag falls and irregular heartbeats; telemedicine reduces travel for routine care. Social apps fight isolation when designed for older eyes and hands.

Risks include surveillance creep, scams, and interfaces that assume youthful dexterity.

Good design involves older users as co-creators, not afterthoughts. Technology should add dignity, not dependency.

writingLibrary.title: 职业倦怠
writingLibrary.prompt:
What causes burnout among young professionals, and how can it be prevented?

(参考题型: Beyond "Just Rest")
writingLibrary.essay:
Burnout is not fixed by weekend yoga alone. Chronic overload, lack of control, and unfair recognition systems drive exhaustion.

Prevention requires organizational fixes: realistic deadlines, manager training, and workload transparency. Individuals benefit from boundaries, but boundaries fail in toxic cultures.

Healthy workplaces treat energy as a managed resource.

writingLibrary.title: 开放获取学术
writingLibrary.prompt:
Should publicly funded research be free to read?

(参考题型: Knowledge as Public Good)
writingLibrary.essay:
If taxes fund research, paywalls restrict who can build on results. Open access accelerates innovation in poorer institutions and countries.

Publishers still need sustainable models—transformational agreements, institutional repositories, and fair APCs.

The principle is simple: knowledge financed by the public should return to the public.

writingLibrary.title: 极简主义生活方式
writingLibrary.prompt:
Is minimalism a solution to overconsumption or a luxury trend?

(参考题型: Less as a Practice)
writingLibrary.essay:
Minimalism promises clarity through fewer possessions. Environmentally, buying less reduces waste and carbon.

Critics note that curated minimalism often requires wealth to "choose" less; low-income families never had excess to reject.

The useful core is intentional consumption, not aesthetic scarcity. Question each purchase: does this serve a life goal or an image?

Enough is a radical, learnable standard.

writingLibrary.title: 危机中的科学传播
writingLibrary.prompt:
How should scientists communicate during public health crises?

(参考题型: Uncertainty, Spoken Clearly)
writingLibrary.essay:
During crises, people need guidance before certainty is complete. Scientists must explain uncertainty without appearing confused.

Clear briefings, visible evidence updates, and admission of mistakes build more trust than false confidence.

Journalists and platforms share responsibility for context, not only speed.

Trust is built in the briefing room long before it is needed.

writingLibrary.title: 职业教育地位
writingLibrary.prompt:
Why does vocational education deserve more respect?

(参考题型: Skill Is Not Second-Class)
writingLibrary.essay:
Economies need technicians as much as theorists. Vocational paths often lead to stable, well-paid work sooner.

Stigma remains strong in some societies, pushing unsuitable students into overcrowded academic tracks.

Solutions include dual education systems, industry partnerships, and transparent career data.

Prestige should follow competence, not only classroom length.

writingLibrary.title: 游戏化学习的边界
writingLibrary.prompt:
When does gamification help or harm learning?

(参考题型: Points vs. Understanding)
writingLibrary.essay:
Badges and streaks can nudge early engagement. Overused, they shift attention from mastery to scores, and learners quit when rewards disappear.

Effective gamification supports practice schedules and visible progress, not circus effects.

Educators should ask: does this design deepen effort or only decorate it?

writingLibrary.title: 全球供应链脆弱性
writingLibrary.prompt:
What have recent disruptions taught us about global supply chains?

(参考题型: Efficiency vs. Resilience)
writingLibrary.essay:
Just-in-time systems cut costs until shocks exposed their fragility. Semiconductors, medical supplies, and energy all showed single-point failures.

Firms now weigh resilience: diversified suppliers, strategic stockpiles, and regional capacity.

Trade remains beneficial; naive optimization does not. Robust systems plan for the unexpected decade, not only the average year.

writingLibrary.title: 城市噪音治理
writingLibrary.prompt:
How can cities reduce harmful noise while staying vibrant?

(参考题型: Soundscapes for Health)
writingLibrary.essay:
Chronic noise disrupts sleep and raises stress, yet cities thrive on activity. Solutions include quieter road surfaces, night freight limits, green buffers, and zoning that separates nightlife from bedrooms.

Enforcement and measurement matter as much as slogans.

A livable city is not silent; it is intentionally designed.

writingLibrary.title: 研究生扩招与就业
writingLibrary.prompt:
How should graduate enrollment relate to job markets?

(参考题型: Degrees and Doors)
writingLibrary.essay:
Expanding master's programs can raise national skills or delay employment without adding value.

Alignment with industry needs, funded research slots, and honest career data help students choose wisely.

Society benefits from advanced training only when quality scales with quantity.

writingLibrary.title: 短视频与注意力经济
writingLibrary.prompt:
Who profits when attention is the product?

(参考题型: Eyes for Sale)
writingLibrary.essay:
Free platforms monetize watch time. Designers compete for fragments of attention with autoplay and infinite scroll.

Users "pay" with data and focus. Awareness helps, but structural change—ad transparency, time tools, child protections—matters more than individual heroism.

Attention is finite infrastructure of a mind. Spend it like money.

writingLibrary.title: 绿色金融
writingLibrary.prompt:
Can finance drive environmental goals?

(参考题型: Capital with Conditions)
writingLibrary.essay:
Green bonds and sustainability-linked loans can fund cleaner energy. Critics warn of greenwashing when standards are weak.

Credible impact needs third-party verification, clear metrics, and penalties for misses.

Money already shapes the physical world. The task is steering it honestly.

writingLibrary.title: 跨文化团队管理
writingLibrary.prompt:
What makes cross-cultural teams succeed?

(参考题型: Differences as Design)
writingLibrary.essay:
Diverse teams innovate when differences are managed, not ignored. Clear communication norms, explicit decision rules, and rotating meeting times reduce friction.

Psychological safety lets minority voices speak without social cost.

Diversity is raw material; inclusion is the manufacturing process.

writingLibrary.title: 药物与保健品广告
writingLibrary.prompt:
How should health claims in advertising be regulated?

(参考题型: Promises and Proofs)
writingLibrary.essay:
Supplement ads often blur science and suggestion. Regulation should require substantiated claims and ban misleading language.

Public education on basic trial design helps consumers read labels skeptically.

Health markets need trust; trust needs rules.

writingLibrary.title: 历史街区商业化
writingLibrary.prompt:
Can commercialization fund heritage or destroy it?

(参考题型: Shops vs. Memory)
writingLibrary.essay:
Lively streets can pay for roof repairs and craft revival. Yet chains may displace residents and turn culture into costume.

Policies that cap pure tourist retail, support local tenants, and involve communities in planning keep authenticity alive.

Heritage survives when people can still live inside it.

writingLibrary.title: 员工监控技术
writingLibrary.prompt:
Where should workplace monitoring end?

(参考题型: Trust, Verified)
writingLibrary.essay:
Software can track keystrokes and screenshots. Used poorly, it breeds fear and performative busyness.

Prefer outcome-based evaluation, transparent monitoring policies, and limits on invasive tools.

Management without trust is expensive theater.

writingLibrary.title: 体育赛事与城市品牌
writingLibrary.prompt:
Do mega events pay off for host cities?

(参考题型: Stadiums and Stories)
writingLibrary.essay:
Olympics and World Cups can modernize transit and globalize a city brand. Cost overruns and white-elephant venues are common failures.

Honest cost-benefit analysis and legacy planning should precede bids.

A city is not a billboard; residents pay the bills.

writingLibrary.title: 儿童屏幕时间
writingLibrary.prompt:
How much screen time is appropriate for children?

(参考题型: Growing Up Digital)
writingLibrary.essay:
Debates fixate on minutes; content and context matter more. Creative making and video-chat with family differ from passive endless feeds.

Co-viewing and clear device-free sleep windows help. Parents need realistic guidance, not only guilt.

Childhood needs boredom, movement, and unhurried attention.

writingLibrary.title: 远程医疗监管
writingLibrary.prompt:
What regulations does telemedicine need to grow safely?

(参考题型: Care at a Distance)
writingLibrary.essay:
Telemedicine expands access but raises issues of misdiagnosis, prescription abuse, and data breaches.

Licensing across regions, clear standards of care, and secure platforms are essential.

Innovation in health must move at the speed of safety.

writingLibrary.title: 创意产业与版权
writingLibrary.prompt:
How can copyright balance creators and the public?

(参考题型: Fair Use, Fair Pay)
writingLibrary.essay:
Creators need income; society needs quoting, teaching, and remix culture. Over-long copyrights and weak licensing systems harm both sides.

Clear fair-use norms, collective licensing, and transparent platform payouts can rebalance.

Culture is cumulative—rules should honor past work without freezing the future.

writingLibrary.title: 应急志愿组织
writingLibrary.prompt:
What role do volunteers play in disaster response?

(参考题型: Organized Kindness)
writingLibrary.essay:
Volunteers bring speed and local knowledge after disasters. Untrained crowds can also block roads and spread rumors.

Pre-disaster training, credentialing, and clear chains of command turn goodwill into results.

Prepared communities recover faster.

writingLibrary.title: 大学生创业
writingLibrary.prompt:
Is encouraging student entrepreneurship wise?

(参考题型: Start Smart, Not Only Young)
writingLibrary.essay:
Entrepreneurship teaches initiative and market sense. It can also drain savings and derail study when glamorized without support.

Incubators should offer mentors, honest failure narratives, and academic flexibility.

Not everyone must found a company; everyone can learn entrepreneurial thinking.

writingLibrary.title: 空气污染与建筑设计
writingLibrary.prompt:
How can architecture improve urban air quality?

(参考题型: Buildings That Breathe)
writingLibrary.essay:
Indoor air often matters more than outdoor readings. Proper ventilation, low-emission materials, and green facades reduce exposure.

Building codes should require air metrics, not only energy scores.

Healthy air is designed, not wished for.

writingLibrary.title: 翻译技术与外语专业
writingLibrary.prompt:
Will machines make language majors obsolete?

(参考题型: Translators After Translation)
writingLibrary.essay:
Machines handle routine gisting well. Literary nuance, legal stakes, and high-context diplomacy still need humans.

Language programs should emphasize intercultural expertise, subject-matter depth, and AI-assisted workflows.

The major is not dying; its center of gravity is shifting.
